### jvmcontract: claims javac compiles, String and String[] inputs, String, stream and regex models, induction and lemmas, for example 286's decision claim (verification pending)

[`8594e6b7adb1`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/8594e6b7adb1fc631f5dac87cd1fccdf09e5652f) · [log `b811c6ecd366`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/3e8cabab-4a28-4a79-8207-69568d9e8162/b811c6ecd3667145545c1758b8eed5bc7407e79e5697bf4c27ff938d3ab0ea6f.jsonl.gz)

Example 286 (CVE-2022-22968, Spring Framework 5.3.18 to 5.3.19) states its decision claim in Java over the adapter entry allowed(String[] allowedPatterns, String[] disallowedPatterns, String field): a field some disallowed pattern matches ignoring ASCII case is denied, the match written with streams, lambdas and java.util.regex. Until now jvmcontract refused it at the String[] parameters, at the expressions, and at every String, StringBuilder, stream and regex call on the way. With this change the unchanged claim is proved on 5.3.19 and refuted on 5.3.18 and on the constructed mutant at small bounds inline (3 code units and 3 elements: 8 s, 7 s and 6 s in an unoptimized build), each witness run in the harness on a JVM; the frozen bound of 8 is queued.

What a property check gained. A String parameter is a String of its own of at most --max-array-length code units, and a String[] an array of such Strings or nulls. An assumption or assertion the tool's own expression compiler does not take is compiled by javac into a class beside the harness and run as bytecode, as the target is; a witness of such a claim is run in the harness on a JVM, so a refutation rests on Java's own libraries and not on a model. prove --decreases EXPR proves a method that calls itself by induction on a measure: a recursive call on arguments within the assumption and the bound whose measure is smaller is taken to satisfy the property, and any other recursive call ends the check with no verdict. prove --lemmas FILE proves each lemma first and then lets its statement stand in for the calls of its method where the arguments are within the bound it was proved at, the method running as written elsewhere; a method that writes a field or compares its arguments by identity is refused as a lemma's subject.

What the own checker gained. String.substring, indexOf, endsWith, toLowerCase on ASCII (under the stated assumption that the default locale is not Turkish, Azeri or Lithuanian), split at one character and chars; StringBuilder's constructors, length, indexOf, substring, delete and toString; lambdas, method references and four stream model classes run as the loops they stand for; Pattern.quote, String.join, Pattern.compile, matcher and matches as far as a claim states a glob with them, a pattern held as its pieces so that a case-insensitive match and an exact match of lower-cased Strings are one formula; class literals, Class.forName and the class path's loader under a stated assumption, for spring-jcl's logging probes. Each new String method has an evidence record in values::OPERATIONS (String model 3) whose 85 boundary cases give one outcome on the JVM, in the interpreter and in the checker; the interpreter's substring and toLowerCase now return the JDK's objects (the String itself, the literal empty String). What a model takes for granted about the JVM is listed among a statement's assumptions.

Paths. Once more than 1024 paths have been explored (Options::merge_heaps_after), paths whose heaps are not of one shape are merged into the union of their heaps, each first rid of dead locals and unreachable objects; a loop's exit is then a join, and waiting paths are resumed in the order of the loops they are in. Below that count the engine merges as before. The count is a measured compromise: merging heaps from the first path took the values sweep's list totals from 0.07 s to over a minute at 6 lines, since the two sums are then no longer one formula by gate hashing, and waiting for 1024 paths costs example 286's decision 1.7 times its time at 5 code units against 512. An array of computed size is taken within one more than the bound (a table over a bounded String's positions).

Two leaks found by the default run and closed. The new StringBuilder, Class and ArrayList models had been added to gaps::exact_jdk_call, which JBMC's gap listing and the contract reader also ask: JBMC's stubs for those calls would have counted as exact, and a contract for StringBuilder.&lt;init>() was refused. They are now gaps::modelled_jdk_call, the own checker's alone, and a contract given for a modelled call is applied in place of the model, so the three contract tests of lib/tests/integration.rs pass unchanged. And a call the checker has no model of on a builder it holds the content of (append, reverse) now drops that content: a later modelled call on the builder is refused by name instead of answering from stale content.

examples/286-.../proofs/prove.py TASK runs vulnerable-security, fixed-security or mutant-security from target.json and the frozen claim file, on the revision's pinned JARs (each checked against its SHA-256) with the adapter compiled against them, and builds the mutant as sources.lock.json says. proofs/simple-match.contract is the lemma: PatternMatchUtils.simpleMatch on ASCII Strings is the claim's own regular expression, by induction on the pattern's length. These are proofs beside the example route, which runs the verifier on the original artifact alone and still stops at DataBinder's receiver (VF-027); the example's records are not changed in this commit and follow with the results.

### CLAUDE.md: a probe of a prover or model checker may run inline up to 5 minutes and 4 GB, under a cap

[`48e341653f52`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/48e341653f52577631fe8f778ebab83dbfc0fe76) · [log `7ec3c13b23bc`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/3e8cabab-4a28-4a79-8207-69568d9e8162/7ec3c13b23bcc6acf8de525755c3db63847c6ea48cc58275a054f8048b958db9.jsonl.gz)

At the user's request: the 1 GB line between inline runs and verification jobs had agents tuning a checker's memory to fit a quick probe before knowing whether the real proof works (prove-examples, example 287), and real-world claims often need more than 1 GB just to show where a checker stops. A single probe on one claim may now run inline, one at a time, for up to 5 minutes and 4 GB, inside systemd-run --scope with MemoryMax=4G and a timeout, so it cannot take more. A run that needs more is still a job, and the default test run and the tool tier keep their 1 GB. CLAUDE.md and verification/README.md say the same.

### jvmcontract: loops beyond the bound covered by invariants, constant regexes, text as bytes and digits, for example 287's bcrypt claims (verification pending)

[`26a42d401510`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/26a42d4015101c295cc50896bfc8fc9a9a017c92) · [log `7ec3c13b23bc`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/3e8cabab-4a28-4a79-8207-69568d9e8162/7ec3c13b23bcc6acf8de525755c3db63847c6ea48cc58275a054f8048b958db9.jsonl.gz)

Example 287 (CVE-2025-22228: BCrypt.hashpw ignores bytes past 72) asks whether checkpw rejects a password of more than 72 bytes for every valid stored hash. The tool's own checker stopped at the claim's regular expression, at the text-to-bytes calls and at bcrypt's loops, which go round 18, 512, 2^cost and 64 times against --unwind 16. It now runs the claims as they are written. A loop that goes round more often than the bound is covered by an invariant the checker finds and proves by induction (lib/src/bmc/loops.rs: what one iteration writes is set to any value, candidate facts about each written number are dropped until the rest is kept by an iteration, and the loop is shown to end by a counter or said not to be); a verdict names the loops so covered, a violation past one is believed only when its witness, the least violating input, reproduces on a JVM, and otherwise the answer is no verdict with the loop named. Also new: String.matches and Pattern.compile of a constant regular expression with classes, groups, alternatives and counts (lib/src/bmc/regex.rs); String.getBytes(UTF_8), MessageDigest.isEqual, Arrays.copyOf, Integer.parseInt and StringBuilder's charAt and appends (lib/src/bmc/bytes.rs, strings.rs); Object.getClass of an object the run made, String.toString, an initializer that keeps method references, and a throws clause whose condition javac compiles. The solver side defers clauses until a call depends on them, checks lazy divisions only in the cone a question reads, and shares a path's models by pages. The search for the least witness takes at most half the time the run has left, so a violation found late is not lost to it.

The String model is model 4, the reference calls model 2: getBytes, matches and toString have evidence records sampled on the JVM and in the checker (lib/tests/values.rs), the gap scan counts Pattern.compile of a constant in the checker's syntax as reproduced, and the interpreter's String.toString returns the String itself. Tests that relied on a class regex, toString or a builder append being a gap now use forms that still are (a reluctant or possessive quantifier, trim, append(CharSequence), append(long)); the calibration fixture's RegexGate uses a possessive quantifier and its records were remade. New tests: lib/tests/loops.rs (four, on a small fixture with the same loop shapes), three in lib/tests/claims.rs (each model against a definition written out in Java and sampled on a JVM), three unit tests in bits.rs. Verified inline by the default run (python3 lib/tools/test_costs.py run: 34 of 34 passed).

Example 287 has proofs/prove.py, which runs the three security tasks beside the route through the adapter entry the claim names, and a dated note. One capped probe (5 minutes, 4 GiB) proved the byte-array guard claim on 6.3.8 at the route's bound in 250 s with six loops covered; the probe on 6.3.7 found its violating path and ran out of time minimising the witness, and the probe of the security claim through the adapter did not finish. None of these is a receipt. Jobs: 20261116-053832-example-287-fixed-guard-the-byte-array-g and 20261116-053832-example-287-vulnerable-guard-the-byte-ar (through the route), 20261116-053832-example-287-fixed-security-through-the-a, 20261116-053832-example-287-vulnerable-security-through and 20261116-053832-example-287-mutant-security-through-the (prove.py), and 20261116-053833-the-proof-tier-after-example-287-s-engin (the proof tier with --no-fail-fast and VF-018's three heap tests skipped, as VF-030 asks). ### Two modes of a checkout: development, and runtime on a user's machine

[`88f38b478762`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/88f38b47876220ef2e73f70ef6d5569c45b3303f) · [log `a3f2391d6970`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/3e8cabab-4a28-4a79-8207-69568d9e8162/a3f2391d6970f282935bc8d408198d2d91a8ca64dff65e22e90fa4c76d9d67db.jsonl.gz)

/prove-java-change will install a released copy of this repository on a user's machine. That copy must not trace, redact or publish anything, yet the agents working in it follow this repository's procedure, which says to commit with sync.py commit. So the procedure stays one and the checkout decides: llm-dlc/tools/mode.py tells a runtime checkout by a marker file at its root, .in-the-loop-runtime.json (written by the skill's bootstrap, gitignored, a fact about one copy), and anything else is a development checkout that behaves as it always has. IN_THE_LOOP_MODE overrides the marker for tests. A marker that can't be read is an error, never a development checkout, since tracing a user's sessions by mistake would publish them.

In a runtime checkout sync.py does this, decided before it takes its lock or writes anything under its state folder: commit writes the message with an In-The-Loop-Runtime: VERSION sha256:DIGEST trailer naming the release and starts a new change, reading no session; check passes with nothing to check; the hooks that run after every tool call and turn return at once; and every other command (push, upload, scan, sync, review, allow, stamp, langfuse, unpublish, regenerate) refuses and points at llm-dlc/runtime.md. In a development checkout one thing changes: link_commits never stamps a session's trace on a commit that carries the runtime trailer, so a contribution merged from a user's checkout is not credited to whichever session happened to be running when it was authored.

llm-dlc/runtime.md is the new page for the runtime side, starting with the two modes and the procedure for agents in a runtime checkout; CLAUDE.md and llm-dlc/README.md point at it. Examples added in a runtime checkout take numbers 900 to 999, which examples/README.md now reserves, so an update never brings an example with the same number.

Verified: test_mode.py (13 tests, in the cost inventory as unit tier) covers the marker, the override, each runtime command, main's dispatch without the lock, and the unstamped contributed commit. Run for real with IN_THE_LOOP_MODE=runtime: check exits 0, push exits 2 with the reason, hook exits 0 silently. Every Python suite passes (lib/tools/test_costs.py run --only python, 34 of 34 after test_performance.py's copied tool sources gained mode.py), and cargo test --test tiers, the Rust half of the tier lint. The rest of cargo test was not run again: no Rust file changed since the previous commit's full default run.

### A release process with a hash, and the bootstrap that installs a release

[`bd66079171f8`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/bd66079171f867de904ef88709464abbb0664ca9) · [log `a3f2391d6970`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/3e8cabab-4a28-4a79-8207-69568d9e8162/a3f2391d6970f282935bc8d408198d2d91a8ca64dff65e22e90fa4c76d9d67db.jsonl.gz)

/prove-java-change runs on a released copy of this repository, and the copy has to be the one the running skill was released with. A release is therefore one commit, the skill at a version and the repository beside it, pinned to each other by the sha256 digest of the commit's tree, which the skill carries in release.json beside its bootstrap. The pin can't name the commit's id, because it is in that commit, so it names the content: the digest is over one line per file (mode, sha256 of its bytes, path) and leaves out the pin itself and the files sync.py regenerates on every commit (llm-dlc/traces/, llm-dlc/index.json, llm-dlc/README.md), which the pin lists. It is of content only, so the trace lines sync.py adds to a commit's message later leave it as it was.

llm-dlc/tools/release.py cut [VERSION] is the one command a release takes, at any commit and as often as wanted: it writes the version into the plugin and the marketplace, the pin from @'s tree, commits with sync.py commit, and verifies the commit; it refuses while @ holds other uncommitted work. status and verify read the last release back. A release reaches users only when main is pushed with it.

plugins/in-the-loop/skills/prove-java-change/bootstrap.py is the user's side and the one implementation of the digest (release.py loads it). status says where things stand as JSON, install clones the repository with jj into IN_THE_LOOP_HOME (by default ~/.local/share/in-the-loop) and stands on the release, update fetches and rebases the user's commits onto the next release, listing conflicts. A release is found without a tag: through the history of the pin, for the commit that carries this version and digest, accepted only when its tree hashes to the digest again. A checkout is current only when that holds, the working copy descends from the release, and the skill's files in the release are the bytes of the skill that is running. Inside a development checkout the bootstrap answers development and installs nothing. The plugin's manifest and the marketplace entry come back with it, as plugin in-the-loop at 0.4.0; the skill's own page follows in a later commit, and no release is cut yet.

Verified: test_release.py, 11 tests (8 at the tool tier, with git and jj on a made-up repository in a temporary directory): the digest ignores messages and the files left out and sees a changed byte or mode; a commit changed after its digest was taken is no release; install stands on the release rather than the branch's tip, writes the marker and leaves git clean; a skill edited after it was installed blocks; a pin whose release is not in the repository installs nothing and leaves no directory; update moves a local commit onto the next release. On this repository the digest of 5,380 files takes 0.4 s. Every Python suite passes (35 of 35) and cargo test --test tiers; the rest of cargo test was not rerun, no Rust file having changed.

### doctor.py: whether a machine can prove a change, and what blocks it

[`cc7a5bb0fa85`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/cc7a5bb0fa8502a67d0ba5015c23abcaa51e0fdf) · [log `a3f2391d6970`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/3e8cabab-4a28-4a79-8207-69568d9e8162/a3f2391d6970f282935bc8d408198d2d91a8ca64dff65e22e90fa4c76d9d67db.jsonl.gz)

Step 1 of /prove-java-change has to say, in numbers, whether the user's machine is enough, and to tell what no setup can fix from what a setup fixes. llm-dlc/tools/doctor.py measures the machine and looks for the tools, installs and changes nothing, and gives each check one of three levels. Blocking: a proof can't run here; a hardware limit (under 8 GiB of memory, 2 CPUs or 10 GiB of free disk, a margin below the 8-core, 9 GB laptop that is the smallest machine this repository has run on) or an operating system other than Linux is blocking by itself, and so is a missing tool every proof needs (Python 3.11 with jsonschema, git, jj, a Java 25 JDK, cargo, and a Claude Code with the flags the loop uses). Limits: the machine works with less, and the check says what is lost (no JBMC, no systemd user scopes for memory caps, no JDK 21 and 25 under sdkman for replays, no Maven, gh or tmux). Ok otherwise. It exits 1 when something blocks, and --json gives the same as data.

It also proposes a budget, shared out as verification/README.md describes: a reserve for the person and the operating system, one loop's memory cap, and the rest to the verification runner, for whoever sets the machine up to adjust. For this VM (30 vCPUs, 105 GiB) the arithmetic gives the budget that was set here by hand on 2026-11-14: a 13G reserve, 12G for a loop, 80G and 26 CPUs for the runner.

Verified: test_doctor.py, 11 unit tests over made-up machines (which sizes block and which limit, that a limit says what is lost, that the three shares fit in machines from 8 to 512 GiB, the VM's budget, the exit status). Run on this machine: nothing blocking, nothing limiting. Every Python suite passes (36 of 36) and cargo test --test tiers; no Rust file changed, so the rest of cargo test was not rerun.

### prove-loop.sh: a proof loop forked from the session that prepared the example, with that session as its conductor

[`4da1371e024c`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/4da1371e024cd9a56612d5375d9e05211b31df3e) · [log `a3f2391d6970`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/3e8cabab-4a28-4a79-8207-69568d9e8162/a3f2391d6970f282935bc8d408198d2d91a8ca64dff65e22e90fa4c76d9d67db.jsonl.gz)

Step 3 of /prove-java-change. llm-dlc/tools/prove-loop.sh [--fork SESSION] [--memory SIZE] NNN... runs a new templated moonshot of feature-loop.sh, prove-change, over the examples it is given: the instruction of prove-examples, one example per cycle, on Fable 5.2 at high effort, every example given whether an earlier run committed for it or not. With --fork the loop's session starts as a fork of the session that prepared the example: the parent's transcript is found wherever that session ran, copied beside this checkout's sessions for one turn that runs without tools or the repository's hooks, and removed; the fork is then compacted and the cycles follow in it, so the loop needs no brief. The script starts the verification loop for the jobs the proof queues unless one already runs for the same jj repository, gives the queue an hour to clear after the loop ends, and keeps the run's state in llm-dlc/loop-summaries/prove-change/. It works the same in a development and a runtime checkout.

The conductor. The commit below this one (brought into this line from the moonshot workspace, where it was waiting) makes a moonshot's session compact itself at 600k tokens and stops the loop at a compaction with no commit. That rule can't tell hard work going well from a stuck session, and the conductor loop planned for it is superseded: the session that starts a proof loop conducts it. With LOOP_CONDUCTOR set, which prove-loop.sh does, the loop's reader appends the compaction to events.jsonl, lets the turn go on, and waits FEATURE_LOOP_CONDUCTOR_WAIT seconds (900) for a verdict. llm-dlc/tools/conductor.py wait blocks until there is such an event or the loop has ended, and decide N continue|stop --reason answers it. continue lets the turn run to its next compaction and is noted under the cycle's line in the run's record; stop, or silence, ends the turn and the loop as the rule alone does. A turn that ends by itself first takes its question back. Every other loop is unchanged: without LOOP_CONDUCTOR the rule stands as it was.

feature-loop.sh also gains FEATURE_LOOP_UNCAPPED=1, to run with no memory cap on a machine without systemd user scopes, where it otherwise refuses to start; it says so loudly. llm-dlc/runtime.md describes the loop and the conductor, and llm-dlc/README.md lists the loop with the others.

Verified with a stand-in claude, no model called: test_prove_loop.py (8 tool-tier tests, about 6 s) runs prove-loop.sh, feature-loop.sh and the reader for real in a made-up jj repository under a temporary CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR, and checks the fork's arguments and that the parent's copy is removed, the compact, the one-line instruction on claude-fable-5-2 at high effort with --autocompact 600k, a fresh session without --fork, a compaction that goes on at the conductor's word with its note in the record, one that stops at its word, one that stops for want of a verdict, a question taken back, a cycle with no commit, and an example that isn't there. test_conductor.py (10 unit tests) covers the event file and the verdicts. Forking a session that is mid-turn was tried by hand earlier with a real claude on a scratch folder; no real proof loop has been run through this yet. Every Python suite passes (38 of 38) and cargo test --test tiers; no Rust file changed.

### /prove-java-change: the skill

The skill that replaces /verify-bytecode and /add-tla-model, and supersedes the planned conductor loop: plugins/in-the-loop/skills/prove-java-change/SKILL.md, in the plugin in-the-loop beside its bootstrap. It proves a change to Java code on a user's machine in four steps and is kept short on purpose, since it is locked to Fable 5.2 at high effort and runs inside this repository: it says what each step is for and when to stop, and the repository holds the rest. Step 0 asks the bootstrap where it is. Step 1 (set up, verify and measure the machine) is skipped when the checkout is current and doctor.py finds nothing blocking, and otherwise goes to one subagent on Opus; a hardware limit ends the run; the user confirms. Step 2 (assess the change, add the example with its claims, run it once on a JVM) stays in the orchestrating session, because the proof loop is forked from it; the user confirms. Step 3 starts prove-loop.sh --fork with the session's own id and conducts the loop from outside. Step 4 reports each claim as established, refuted or left open and offers to send what the proof added to the tool upstream. The orchestrator decides what it can and asks only for what is the user's.

In this repository the skill is also a project skill: .claude/skills/prove-java-change is a link to its folder in the plugin, so /prove-java-change NNN runs the copy being worked on, the bootstrap answers development, steps 1 and 2 are skipped and the skill goes straight to the loop on an existing example. Installed as a plugin it is /in-the-loop:prove-java-change. llm-dlc/runtime.md opens with a table of the four steps and what each stands on, and the top README has a section for the skill with how to install it.

Two things the page is honest about. release.py status now exits 1 while the skill's folder differs from the last release, because the plugin is installed from the tip of main and a copy of the skill that is not its release's bytes refuses to run: a change to the skill is followed by a cut before main is pushed. And a change that is not public has no route yet: a revision is prepared from a commit on github.com or a published JAR, so a private or uncommitted change is a blocker at step 2, or a fixture when it is small enough to copy; a local repository as a revision's source is the next piece of work, left out here because it changes the downloads policy and the files the running prove-examples loop works in.

Verified: claude plugin validate passes for the marketplace and the plugin; the bootstrap run through the project skill's link answers development with this checkout as home; every Python suite passes (39 of 39) and cargo test --test tiers. Not verified: the skill has not been run, in development mode or installed. That waits for the prove-examples loop to finish, as agreed, since a run starts a second proof loop on this machine.

### feature-loop.sh: a compaction with no commit stops a moonshot only on a conductor's word, or with FEATURE_LOOP_STOP_ON_COMPACT=1

[`2da2110938a7`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/2da2110938a78c1fcb712f3142286334884d0f99) · [log `a3f2391d6970`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/3e8cabab-4a28-4a79-8207-69568d9e8162/a3f2391d6970f282935bc8d408198d2d91a8ca64dff65e22e90fa4c76d9d67db.jsonl.gz)

This line carries a copy (srxmyvov) of the change that made a moonshot compact at 600k tokens and stop at a compaction with no commit. The original, uzporttn in the moonshot workspace, was amended on 2026-11-15 at the user's request: the stop became opt-in, because cycle 2 of the prove-examples run compacted with no commit while making good progress, so the rule would have stopped good work. This commit brings this line to the same behaviour and fits the conductor to it, so that uzporttn can be abandoned at the merge instead of merged.

A moonshot's compaction with no commit since the cycle began, or since the last one, now has three outcomes. With neither setting, it is logged and nothing else happens, as in the amended uzporttn. With FEATURE_LOOP_STOP_ON_COMPACT=1 and no conductor, the turn ends and the loop stops, the old rule. With LOOP_CONDUCTOR, which prove-loop.sh sets, the conductor is asked: its stop ends the turn and the loop, and its continue lets the turn run to the next compaction. What changes for the conductor is its silence: no verdict by the deadline used to stop the loop and now leaves the turn running, with a line in the run's record, unless FEATURE_LOOP_STOP_ON_COMPACT=1 is also set. A conductor that has gone away, such as an orchestrating session the user closed, is then no worse than no conductor, and can't cause the false stop the amendment removed. The question is asked again at the next compaction with no commit. The header of feature-loop.sh, conductor.py's description, llm-dlc/runtime.md and llm-dlc/README.md say the same.

Verified with the stand-in claude: test_prove_loop.py has 11 tool-tier tests (8.5 s), four of them new or changed: silence from the conductor lets the turn go on and is noted under the cycle's line; silence with the rule on stops the loop; feature-loop.sh run by itself, with no conductor, only logs the compaction and the turn runs to its own end; and with the rule on it stops at the compaction. The conductor's continue and stop are tested as before. Every Python suite passes (39 of 39) and cargo test --test tiers. ### /prove-java-change takes a list of changes, orders them by how accessible they are, and prepares without proving with --scaffold-only

[`50c414430a4e`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/50c414430a4eb1ef5c9c12319f20ad09e21cdbd6) · [log `a3f2391d6970`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/3e8cabab-4a28-4a79-8207-69568d9e8162/a3f2391d6970f282935bc8d408198d2d91a8ca64dff65e22e90fa4c76d9d67db.jsonl.gz)

The skill's request is now one change or a list of them. Step 2 understands and sizes every change, orders them with the most accessible first (a proof that lands early can extend the verifier under the later ones), and adds the examples in that order on the next free numbers from 900, so the numbers carry the order and no separate record of it exists. Each example's provenance is the request it came from and its notes hold what the preparation learned, because its proof may start in a session that never saw the preparation. A change that can't be prepared is set aside with its reason and the others go on.

--scaffold-only ends the skill after step 2, with every example a committed, reproducible scaffold (the readiness the examples' index already calls scaffolded) and no proof started. The same request without the flag proves what was prepared: nothing remembers a request, step 2 finds each change's example by its source and revisions and prepares only what has none. Step 3 then gives prove-loop.sh the examples still to prove, in order, in one run (one per cycle, in one session, as before) or, if the user prefers, one example per run with a report between. In a development checkout the examples named are taken in the order given.

New tool llm-dlc/tools/changes.py, read-only: it derives each example's state from its folder alone through examples/tools/targets/workflow.py (unprepared with the reason, prepared, decided, or unknown for an example with no target sidecar), lists a runtime checkout's examples 900 to 999 by number or the named ones in the order given, and with --pending prints the numbers still to prove as prove-loop.sh's arguments. A claim left open keeps its example to prove; a refuted claim decides it. llm-dlc/runtime.md has a new section, Many changes and preparing without proving, and the top README and llm-dlc/README.md's layout mention the list, the flag and the tool.

Verified: test_changes.py (15 unit tests on copies of the made-up target fixture with hand-written receipts) covers each state, the order, --pending and that nothing is written; two new tests in test_prove_loop.py run prove-loop.sh on three examples against the stand-in claude and check one cycle each, in the order given, in one session, and that a cycle with no commit leaves the examples after it untouched. The Python half of the default run passes (40 of 40 suites), cargo test --test tiers passes, claude plugin validate passes for the plugin and the marketplace, and every relative link and anchor on the edited pages resolves. Not verified: the skill itself has not been run by a model on a real list; only the tools under it are tested. The skill's folder changed, so a release is owed and follows in the next commit.

### /prove-java-change checks what else Claude Code has loaded, and the sessions it starts load only the checkout

[`fe74a7d1edfd`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/fe74a7d1edfd82eaed4bc65c62c924d328139cf5) · [log `a3f2391d6970`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/3e8cabab-4a28-4a79-8207-69568d9e8162/a3f2391d6970f282935bc8d408198d2d91a8ca64dff65e22e90fa4c76d9d67db.jsonl.gz)

Step 1 of the skill now checks the user's Claude Code setup on every run. New tool llm-dlc/tools/claude_setup.py: check prints a warning that any extraneous context from external sources may lead to unexpected results, then lists what the session running it has loaded besides the plugin and the checkout (other plugins, MCP servers and claude.ai connectors, memory files, skills, agents, commands, hooks, managed settings). It asks Claude Code itself: two one-word sessions on the smallest model, without tools or a transcript, one started as the user's session was (its directory and launch flags, read from the process CLAUDE_PID names) and one clean in the checkout, compared by what each reports at start-up; memory files, hooks and the plugins Claude Code's own listing calls enabled are added from disk. It prints names and paths only, never a setting's value.

Disabling is done by launch flags, not by editing the user's configuration, so nothing has to be put back: --setting-sources project,local, --strict-mcp-config, ENABLE_CLAUDEAI_MCP_SERVERS=false, and claudeMdExcludes for the memory files of the user and of the directories above the checkout. In a runtime checkout every session the skill starts now uses them (loop-common.sh's isolation: the proof loop's fork, compactions and cycles, and the verification loop's runs), and check proves on the machine that such a launch answers. The session the user is already in can't unload what it holds, so when anything is listed the skill offers the one command check prints (claude_setup.py launch: a clean session in the checkout, on Fable 5.2 at high effort, where the skill runs as the checkout's project skill) or, not recommended, to continue as it is. prove-loop.sh --no-isolation starts the loop's sessions as a plain claude for a machine where a clean launch does not work. A development checkout's loops are unchanged, and check refuses there because its hooks would trace the probes.

Verified: test_claude_setup.py (21 tests, the check itself against a stand-in claude and made-up directories) and two new tests in test_prove_loop.py (in a runtime checkout all five sessions of a run carry the clean flags; with --no-isolation or in a development checkout none does). With the real Claude Code 2.1.325, from scratch directories: the flags leave no MCP server, connector, user skill or plugin in the start-up report, a memory file excluded by path is not read while the checkout's own is, the checkout's project skills still load, the login still works, and launch started from another project answers with the checkout's memory and not that project's. The Python half of the default run passes (41 of 41 suites), cargo test --test tiers passes, claude plugin validate passes, and the edited pages' links resolve. Not verified: whether --setting-sources alone drops the user's own memory file (Claude Code's documentation does not say, and this machine has none, hence the exclusion by path); a real proof loop under the clean flags; and the skill's new step run by a model. A known limit, documented: a non-interactive probe was seen to report no connectors in a directory that has a memory file, where an interactive session has them, so the skill also adds what the session sees in its own context. The skill's folder changed, so a release follows.

### feature-loop.sh: a templated moonshot keeps an item for as many cycles as it takes, until a judge outside the session finds it finished, and "item" stops the loop once the item under way is

[`46b49aece682`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/46b49aece68286148430cff7eaeaf5481bc83183) · [log `a3f2391d6970`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/3e8cabab-4a28-4a79-8207-69568d9e8162/a3f2391d6970f282935bc8d408198d2d91a8ca64dff65e22e90fa4c76d9d67db.jsonl.gz)

At the user's request: complex examples can take more than one cycle, but a templated moonshot gave each item exactly one, moving on as soon as a cycle committed (prove-examples left 286 with tasks open), and "stop" could only end the loop after a cycle, not after an example.

Now, after each commit of a templated moonshot, a judge outside the session decides whether the item is finished: a separate claude -p call (FEATURE_LOOP_JUDGE_MODEL, claude-sonnet-5-5 by default) with no tools, only the user's settings and no transcript reads the cycle's final report and commit messages and answers ITEM: finished (the goal is met, or what is left needs a person or only waits on jobs) or ITEM: continue (the session itself can still make real progress). Nothing is added to the moonshot's own session, so its instruction stays the only thing it is given. An unfinished item gets the next cycle with the same instruction; an unclear answer moves on, as before. The record keeps the verdict and its reason under each commit line, and a later run resumes at the first item that has no commit or whose last verdict was continues. FEATURE_LOOP_ITEM_CYCLES caps an item's cycles in a run (no cap by default, the user's choice), and FEATURE_LOOP_ITEM_JUDGE=0 restores one cycle per item. Typing "item" in the loop's terminal ends the run once the item under way is finished, however many cycles that takes; a count typed after it replaces it. loop_stats.py reads the new record header and verdicts, so an item the judge left open counts as attempted, not done, and the verdict is not published as a column.

Verified: test_loop_stats (22, two new) and test_runs pass, and the cost lint agrees. End to end, in a scratch jj repo with a stand-in claude that commits and answers as the judge from a script, the patched script (its own three-item list, no systemd scope): the judge kept item 1 for two cycles and the run went on to 2 and 3 and ended with no items left; a record whose last verdict was continues resumed at that item; an unclear answer moved on; a cap of 2 moved on after two continues; FEATURE_LOOP_ITEM_JUDGE=0 kept the old header and one cycle per item; a bad cap exits 2; and "item" typed during cycle 1, on a private tmux server, ended the run after cycle 2, once the judge found item 1 finished. Three real judge calls on made-up reports answered finished for a decided example, continue for one with work the session could do, and finished for one blocked on a person's decision.

### feature-loop.sh: a conductor judges each cycle, an item that waits on its proof lets the next one start, and the loop asks before it changes items

[`d7cbe1334d14`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/d7cbe1334d145209fec278b655703c9df1476f35) · [log `a3f2391d6970`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/3e8cabab-4a28-4a79-8207-69568d9e8162/a3f2391d6970f282935bc8d408198d2d91a8ca64dff65e22e90fa4c76d9d67db.jsonl.gz)

This folds the moonshot branch into the /prove-java-change line. The commit below this one is a duplicate of tlzowkqv (workspace moonshot: an item keeps a templated moonshot until a judge outside the session finds it finished), with its six conflicts against this line resolved; this commit reconciles and extends it. The user asked on 2026-11-16 for everything about moonshot loops from the moonshot and conductor branches to be folded in here, for the loop to be run by a watcher session, and for a loop that goes on while an example waits on its final proof.

With a conductor directory (LOOP_CONDUCTOR, which prove-loop.sh sets) the conductor is the judge: after each commit the loop asks it whether the item is finished, takes another cycle, or only waits on the verification jobs it queued, and falls back on tlzowkqv's own judge (Sonnet, now with the third answer) when no verdict comes in FEATURE_LOOP_JUDGE_WAIT seconds. An item that waits is left: the loop takes the next one meanwhile, and whenever it leaves an item it first returns to the earliest waiting one whose jobs are in (conductor.py unfinished reads the queue and matches jobs to examples by their outputs or title). When only waiting items are left it waits for the first to come in. FEATURE_LOOP_CONTINUE_WHILE_PROVING=0, or prove-loop.sh --wait-for-proofs, keeps the loop on the item instead; the default is on. Between two items the loop asks the conductor whether to stop there, and waits longer while the run's merge-queue names a workspace the conductor is to merge first. The conductor can leave command lines (stop, item, counts) that the loop applies as if typed in its terminal, and the loop notes where it is as events (cycle-start, item, proofs).

So that a merge between two examples can't rewrite the script under the loop, feature-loop.sh and prove-loop.sh now run from a private copy of themselves. prove-loop.sh gains --session SESSION, which continues an existing session instead of forking one, and records its pid in run.json. In a runtime checkout the judge takes the clean launch flags instead of --setting-sources user. loop_stats.py reads the waiting verdict as an item left open, and knows the new endings.

Verified: test_prove_loop.py runs the loop against a stand-in claude, now also a stand-in judge and a made-up job queue (26 tests): the watcher's verdict keeps or ends an example, silence falls back on the judge, an example that waits lets the next start and is taken up again when its jobs are in (order 901, 902, 901, 903), the loop waits when only waiting examples are left, waiting with nothing outstanding is another cycle, --wait-for-proofs removes the third answer, a stop between examples and a queued merge's longer wait, a command line, --session, and a script rewritten mid-run that does not affect the loop. test_conductor.py has five new tests (15). The Python half of the default run passes, 41 of 41 suites. Not verified: any of this with a real model in the loop; the Rust tests were not run (nothing in lib/ changed). The pages (runtime.md, the skill) still describe the previous design and are rewritten with the watcher in the next commit, which also cuts the release.

### /prove-java-change is started by a watcher on Opus 5.5, which starts each stage in a session of its own and watches the proof loop

[`142e511a3aef`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/142e511a3aef80e8b99b41b2fa7f42e8497f9db0) · [log `a3f2391d6970`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/3e8cabab-4a28-4a79-8207-69568d9e8162/a3f2391d6970f282935bc8d408198d2d91a8ca64dff65e22e90fa4c76d9d67db.jsonl.gz)

The skill's session no longer does the work. It is the run's watcher (Opus 5.5, high effort; the user set the models on 2026-11-16) and starts, in order: the setup of the machine (a new session, Opus 5.5 high), the evaluation and ordering of the changes (the fixed session, Fable 5.2 medium), the setup of the examples from the evaluation's plan (a new session, Opus 5.5 high), and the moonshot loop over them, which continues the fixed session at high effort. Beside them it keeps a verification loop (Sonnet 5.5) running for the jobs the sessions queue. In a development checkout the watcher goes straight to the loop on the examples named, which is how every moonshot over examples is run from now on.

llm-dlc/tools/watch.py is the watcher's tool: stage evaluate|setup (a headless session on its model and effort, clean in a runtime checkout), verification start|stop|status, loop (prove-loop.sh detached, with --session), wait (blocks until a question of the loop's, a proof that came in, the loop's end, or a summary when the interval has passed: 600 s by default, set with interval), summary and status (from llm-dlc/watch-summary-template.md, with what changed since the last summary first: examples that changed state, claims answered, commits, jobs queued or in; then the loop, the example under way, the verification jobs and what needs attention, such as a session silent for 20 minutes), merge add|done|list (workspaces the user asked to have merged between two examples), stop-after example|cycle|never, and proof NNN (the shell that waits on one example's proof while the loop works on the next). llm-dlc/prove-plan-template.md is the plan the evaluation fills in and the setup turns into examples.

SKILL.md is rewritten for the watcher, and llm-dlc/runtime.md has its section (the stages' briefs, watching the loop, the three questions and their defaults, merging between examples, what the watcher may fix); README.md and llm-dlc/README.md follow. claude_setup.py's clean launch now defaults to Opus 5.5, the watcher's model.

Verified against stand-ins only: test_watch.py (20 tests: a made-up checkout, a stand-in claude, a queue that is a file), one test in test_prove_loop.py in which watch.py reads the run a real prove-loop.sh wrote, the Python default run (42 of 42 suites), the Rust tier test, claude plugin validate, and every link and anchor of the pages touched. No real model has run the skill, a stage or the loop under this design. The release that carries this is cut in the next commit.

`/prove-java-change` now takes a list of changes and a `--scaffold-only` flag, committed as `yvvkzplr` and cut as release 0.5.0 (`vuxlvnqz`) in the side workspace. Nothing is merged or pushed, and no model has run the new skill text on a real list yet; only the tools under it are tested.

**How it behaves**
- **A list:** step 2 reads and sizes every change first, then orders them with the most accessible first, and says why in a line each. A change that can't be prepared is set aside with its reason, and the others go on.
- **The order:** examples are added in that order on the next free numbers from 900, so the numbers are the order. No separate record of it is kept.
- **`--scaffold-only`:** the skill stops after step 2. Each example is committed with its revisions built, the change run once on a JVM and its claims frozen, and no proof has started.
- **Same request without the flag:** nothing remembers the request. Step 2 matches each change to an existing example by its source and revisions, keeps it, and prepares only what has none. Step 3 then proves whatever is still undecided.
- **One run or one at a time:** at the step 2 confirmation the skill asks which. One run proves the examples one after another in one session, as the moonshot loop does today. One at a time is one example per run, with a report and your go-ahead between.
